study.title: Judges 2 - God's warning, apostasy, and discipline
study.overview: Judges 2 summarizes the pattern that will rule out the whole book: God was faithful to the covenant, Israel failed to obey, idolatry brought discipline, and the Lord in mercy lifted up judges to deliver the people for a time. The chapter begins with the rebuke of the angel of the LORD in Bokchim and concludes by explaining why the neighboring nations were not removed immediately: they would serve as proof to reveal whether Israel would continue walking in the way of the LORD or not.

outline.title: The rebuke in Boquim
outline.explanation: The angel of the LORD recalls the deliverance of Egypt, the gift of the land, and the demand of the covenant: Israel should not make a covenant with the peoples of the earth, nor to tolerate their altars. Disobedience is already treated as a breach of alliance, and the response of the people is crying, regret and sacrifice, indicating guilt awareness, although the text still does not show a lasting reform.

outline.title: The generation of Joshua and the emergence of a new generation
outline.explanation: The narrator returns to the period of Joshua to show the contrast between the fidelity of that time and the later infidelity. Joshua dies, the ancient generation also disappears, and a generation arises that did not know the Lord or his works, a sign of spiritual and historical failure in the transmission of faith.

outline.title: Idolatry, discipline and mercy repeated
outline.explanation: Israel proceeds to do what is bad, serving the Baalins and Canaanite deities. The LORD reacts with anger and oppression through enemies, but also raises judges to deliver the people. Still, the liberation is temporary: after the death of the judge, the people again corrupt themselves, showing a cycle of rebellion and partial relief.

outline.title: God's purpose in leaving the nations
outline.explanation: God declares that he will no longer cast out the nations left by Joshua, because Israel has transgressed the covenant. These nations will remain as proof: they will reveal whether the people will obey the way of the LORD or not. Thus, what seems to be delay or limitation is also God's pedagogical judgment on the infidelity of Israel.

study.context: The chapter works as theological and historical introduction to the book of Judges. He resumes the transition between Joshua's generation and the later generation, explaining why life in Canaan would not become a peaceful and continuous possession. The text shows that coexistence with the remaining peoples and their cults was not neutral: it became an occasion of temptation, trial and discipline. The focus of the chapter is not to inform many political details, but to expose the moral and spiritual relationship between Israel's infidelity and the judgments of the Lord.
study.theology: Judges 2 teaches that God's covenant is real and serious: the grace that brought Israel out of Egypt did not overturn the requirement of obedience. Idolatry appears as spiritual adultery, that is, abandonment of the LORD in favor of false gods. The divine judgment is not whim, but a just answer to the breaking of the covenant. At the same time, the raising of judges reveals God's compassion: he disciplines, but does not immediately abandon his people. The chapter also highlights the generational responsibility in the instruction of faith; when a generation fails to know the Lord and his works, the spiritual ruin becomes probable. Finally, the permanence of the nations shows that God can use even the resistance of the environment as an instrument of proof to reveal the fidelity or infidelity of his people.

scholarViews.insight: Matthew Henry notes that this chapter brings together the contents of the whole book: fidelity under Joshua, apostasy after him, God's judgment, mercy in sending deliverers and, finally, the limit imposed on Israel's successes because of divine wrath.

Adam Clarke understands that the expression about not expelling the nations quickly indicates that God did not remove all the inhabitants immediately because, if he had done so, Israel would probably have relaxed even more and forgotten his Deliverer; the permanence of these nations also served as an occasion for trial.

questions: What does the cry of the people in Boquim reveal about true repentance and only emotional repentance?
Why can a new generation come to "not knowing the Lord" even living among the people of the covenant?
In what practical ways does the Christian heart still run the risk of replacing fidelity to God with modern idols?
study.practice: This chapter calls the church to a faith transmitted with memory and obedience. It is necessary to teach the next generations not only biblical information, but the works of God and the meaning of his covenant. It is also necessary to watch against compromises that dilute fidelity to the LORD, because small concessions can become spiritual traps. When there is discipline of God, the right answer is not only emotion, but repentance accompanied by concrete return to obedience. And when God permits difficult trials, this should be received as a call to perseverance and faithfulness, not as a reason to abandon the way.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text provided already contains the main interpretation of the chapter, so it is not necessary to resort to external data. The commentators' notes are in English and have been summarized in Portuguese without a long quote. The exact scope of the expression about God "if you repent" in verse 18 is presented as a language accommodated to the human way of speaking, following the given note, without pretense to solve all theological issues beyond what the text itself and the notes allow.
